plant.description:
Brief Description (Appearance, Habitat, and Where Commonly Found)
• Appearance: The Sweet Pea is a climbing annual vine that uses thin, curling tendrils to wrap around supports and climb. It is characterized by its winged stems, paired oval leaflets, and highly fragrant, butterfly-shaped flowers that bloom in a wide variety of colors, including shades of pink, purple, red, white, and blue.
• Habitat and Where Commonly Found: Native to the Mediterranean region—specifically Sicily, southern Italy, and the Aegean Islands—it naturally thrives in cool, mild climates with well-draining soil and full sun. Today, it is widely cultivated across the globe and is most commonly found in home gardens, where it is frequently grown on trellises, fences, and arches as a popular ornamental and cut flower.

toxins.name: Aminopropionitriles (specifically beta-aminopropionitrile or BAPN)
toxins.description: Aminopropionitrile (BAPN) is the toxic principle the ASPCA names for this plant. It is a lathyrogen that inhibits the enzyme lysyl oxidase, disrupting the cross-linking of collagen and elastin (the chronic condition known as "lathyrism"). This effect is documented in grazing livestock such as horses, for which the ASPCA classifies Sweet Pea as toxic. The ASPCA classifies the same plant as non-toxic to cats, and no authoritative feline source documents lathyrism or related signs in cats.
toxins.concentration_notes: Per the ASPCA, Sweet Pea is non-toxic to cats. The aminopropionitrile content is the basis for the plant's documented toxicity in horses, not cats.

symptoms.name: Loss of appetite
symptoms.notes: Listed by Pet Poison Helpline among the first signs after sweet pea ingestion in pets.

symptoms.name: Lethargy and weakness
symptoms.notes: Reflects the neuromuscular effects of the lathyrogen BAPN; documented mainly in grazing animals.

symptoms.name: Neuromuscular signs (stumbling, lameness, circling)
symptoms.onset: Delayed; associated with large or repeated ingestion.
symptoms.notes: Classic lathyrism-type signs; cat-specific reports are scarce.

symptoms.name: Seizures
symptoms.notes: Reported in severe cases across species; seek veterinary care immediately.

treatments.name: Emesis Induction and Activated Charcoal
treatments.description: If the ingestion was recent, the veterinarian will medically induce vomiting to remove the plant material from the stomach before it can be fully digested34. This is often followed by administering a dose of activated charcoal, which binds to any remaining toxins in the gastrointestinal tract and prevents them from being absorbed into the bloodstream.
treatments.notes: You should never attempt to induce vomiting at home unless explicitly instructed by a veterinarian, as doing so incorrectly can cause significant injury.

treatments.name: Intravenous (IV) Fluid Therapy
treatments.description: The veterinary team will administer IV fluids to rehydrate the cat, support blood pressure, and maintain proper organ function.
treatments.notes: This intervention is particularly critical for Sweet Pea poisoning, as the plant's toxins trigger vomiting and diarrhea that can lead to significant dehydration.

treatments.name: Anti-emetics and Gastroprotectants
treatments.description: The veterinarian will administer medications to stop nausea and vomiting (anti-emetics) alongside gastroprotectants or antacids to soothe the digestive tract.
treatments.notes: This supportive care is essential to keep the cat comfortable while the toxins pass through its system and to prevent further fluid loss from ongoing vomiting and diarrhea.

treatments.name: Anticonvulsant Therapy
treatments.description: If the cat's nervous system is affected, the veterinarian will administer standard anticonvulsant medications (such as barbiturates or benzodiazepines) to control tremors or seizures.
treatments.notes: While mild exposures to Sweet Pea typically only cause gastrointestinal upset, consuming large amounts can cause severe poisoning resulting in seizures1. This treatment is utilized if the toxicity escalates to a neurological emergency.

name: Sweet Pea
description: Sweet Pea (Lathyrus odoratus) is a fragrant climbing vine whose risk to cats is genuinely disputed: the ASPCA lists Sweet Pea (under Lathyrus latifolius) as non-toxic to cats, while Pet Poison Helpline treats sweet peas as toxic plants. The plant — especially its seeds and seed pods — contains beta-aminopropionitrile (BAPN), a lathyrogen neurotoxin that can cause "lathyrism" with weakness and neuromuscular signs after large or repeated ingestion, although documented poisonings involve mainly grazing animals and cat-specific cases are scarce. Because the danger cannot be ruled out, treat it with caution: a nibbled leaf is unlikely to harm a cat, but do not let cats chew the plant, and keep seeds and pods out of reach. Do not confuse it with the edible garden pea (Pisum sativum).
safetyNotes: Authorities disagree: the ASPCA lists Sweet Pea (Lathyrus latifolius) as non-toxic to cats, while Pet Poison Helpline treats sweet peas (Lathyrus spp.) as toxic; this entry is graded cautious to reflect that uncertainty
Toxic compound: beta-aminopropionitrile (BAPN), a lathyrogen concentrated in seeds and seed pods; it inhibits lysyl oxidase (collagen/elastin cross-linking) and can cause neurolathyrism
Documented lathyrism cases involve mainly grazing animals after substantial or repeated ingestion; cat-specific poisoning data is scarce
Keep seeds and seed pods out of reach and discourage chewing; a single nibbled leaf is unlikely to cause harm
Contact a veterinarian if a cat eats seeds or pods, or shows weakness, stumbling, or other neuromuscular signs
